claim: Mice with loxP sites flanking exons 11 and 13 (Pkd2fl/fl) of the Pkd2 gene were crossed with tamoxifen-inducible Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice, producing a Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 line.
source: Mice with loxP sites flanking exons 11 and 13 (Pkd2fl/fl) of the Pkd2 gene were crossed with tamoxifen-inducible Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice, producing a Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 line.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the mouse model generation, supported by the experimental procedures described in the manuscript.

claim: Genotyping was performed using a 3-primer (a, b, c) strategy to identify wild-type (in C57BL/6J), floxed and deleted PKD2 alleles.
source: Genotyping was performed using a 3-primer (a, b, c) strategy to identify wild-type (in C57BL/6J), floxed and deleted PKD2 alleles.
evidence: This describes the genotyping methodology used in the study.

claim: PCR of genomic DNA from mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of wild-type mice that lack loxP sites produced a 232 bp transcript.
source: PCR of genomic DNA from mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of wild-type mice that lack loxP sites produced a 232 bp transcript (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl mouse arteries and aorta produced a transcript of 318 bp, which arose from primers a and b.
source: Tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl mouse arteries and aorta produced a transcript of 318 bp, which arose from primers a and b (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PCR amplified a 209 bp transcript in vasculature from tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice due to primers a and c, confirming loss of the primer b annealing site.
source: PCR amplified a 209 bp transcript in vasculature from tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice due to primers a and c, confirming loss of the primer b annealing site.
evidence: This is supported by experimental PCR data and confirms successful recombination.

claim: PCR of vasculature in Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 arteries also produced a faint 318 bp band, suggesting that PKD2 is expressed in vascular wall cell types other than myocytes where DNA would not undergo recombination.
source: PCR of vasculature in Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 arteries also produced a faint 318 bp band, suggesting that PKD2 is expressed in vascular wall cell types other than myocytes where DNA would not undergo recombination (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on PCR data showing residual PKD2 signal in knockout arteries.

claim: RT-PCR was performed on RNA extracted from arterial myocytes (~500 cells) that had been individually harvested from mesenteric arteries of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl and tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice.
source: RT-PCR was performed on RNA extracted from arterial myocytes (~500 cells) that had been individually harvested from mesenteric arteries of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl and tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology for RT-PCR analysis.

claim: Arterial myocyte cDNA from both genotypes amplified transcripts for both actin and myosin heavy chain 11, a smooth muscle-specific marker.
source: Arterial myocyte cDNA from both genotypes amplified transcripts for both actin and myosin heavy chain 11, a smooth muscle-specific marker (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A, confirming smooth muscle cell identity.

claim: Products for PECAM, an endothelial cell marker, and aquaporin 4, an astrocyte marker, were not amplified, suggesting that the isolated mRNA was from pure smooth muscle.
source: In contrast, products for PECAM, an endothelial cell marker, and aquaporin 4, an astrocyte marker, were not amplified, suggesting that the isolated mRNA was from pure smooth muscle (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on RT-PCR data showing absence of endothelial and astrocyte markers.

claim: PKD2 primers were designed to anneal to a sequence in exons 9/10 (forward) and 13 (reverse), which span the recombination site.
source: PKD2 primers were designed to anneal to a sequence in exons 9/10 (forward) and 13 (reverse), which span the recombination site (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the primer design strategy for detecting PKD2 knockout.

claim: Transcripts for PKD2 were amplified by cDNA from arterial myocytes of Pkd2fl/fl mice, but not arterial myocytes of Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice.
source: Transcripts for PKD2 were amplified by cDNA from arterial myocytes of Pkd2fl/fl mice, but not arterial myocytes of Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A, demonstrating successful PKD2 knockout at the transcript level.

claim: Tamoxifen induces PKD2 knockout in arterial myocytes of the Pkd2fl/fl:smCre+ mice.
source: These data indicate that tamoxifen induces PKD2 knockout in arterial myocytes of the Pkd2fl/fl:smCre+ mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RT-PCR data showing absence of PKD2 transcripts in tamoxifen-treated knockout mice.

claim: In mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice, PKD2 protein was ~25.3% and 32.6%, respectively of that in Pkd2fl/fl controls.
source: In mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice, PKD2 protein was ~25.3% and 32.6%, respectively of that in Pkd2fl/fl controls (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in the figures.

claim: TRPC6, TRPM4, and ANO1 channels and PKD1, which can form a complex with PKD2, were similar between genotypes.
source: In contrast, TRPC6, TRPM4, and ANO1 channels and PKD1, which can form a complex with PKD2 (Qian et al., 1997; Tsiokas et al., 1997), were similar between genotypes (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data and cites previous studies showing PKD1-PKD2 interaction.

claim: CaV1.2 protein was similar in mesenteric arteries, but slightly higher (~25.6%) in hindlimb arteries of Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice.
source: CaV1.2 protein was similar in mesenteric arteries, but slightly higher (~25.6%) in hindlimb arteries of Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1 – figure supplement B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data.

claim: In aorta of Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice, PKD2 protein was ~46.8% of that in Pkd2fl/fl, whereas CaV1.2 and PKD1 were similar.
source: In aorta of Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice, PKD2 protein was ~46.8% of that in Pkd2fl/fl, whereas CaV1.2 and PKD1 were similar (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification data from aorta.

claim: Piezo1, angiotensin II type one receptors and GPR68 have been proposed to act as vascular mechanosensors.
source: Piezo1, angiotensin II type one receptors and GPR68 have been proposed to act as vascular mechanosensors (Li et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2018; Schleifenbaum et al., 2014; Blodow et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Piezo1, angiotensin II type one receptors and GPR68 proteins were similar in mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice.
source: Piezo1, angiotensin II type one receptors and GPR68 proteins were similar in mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: α-adrenergic receptor subtypes 1A, 1B and 1D were similar in mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice.
source: α-adrenergic receptor subtypes 1A, 1B and 1D were also measured and all were similar in mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: PKD2 protein was present in myocytes of intact arteries and in isolated myocytes of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl control mice, but absent in myocytes of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice.
source: Immunofluorescence demonstrated that PKD2 protein was present in myocytes of intact arteries and in isolated myocytes of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl control mice, but absent in myocytes of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: PKD2 protein was present in endothelial cells of both tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mouse arteries.
source: In contrast, PKD2 protein was present in endothelial cells of both tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mouse arteries (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data showing PKD2 in endothelial cells of both genotypes.

claim: PKD2 detected in Western blots of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mouse arteries is protein present in cell types other than myocytes that would not be targeted by the smooth muscle-specific Cre.
source: These data indicate that PKD2 detected in Western blots of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mouse arteries is protein present in cell types other than myocytes that would not be targeted by the smooth muscle-specific Cre.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of Western blot and immunofluorescence data.

claim: PKD2 is expressed in myocytes of mesenteric and hindlimb arteries and aorta.
source: These results indicate that PKD2 is expressed in myocytes of mesenteric and hindlimb arteries and aorta and that tamoxifen treatment of Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice selectively abolishes PKD2 expression in myocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined RT-PCR, Western blot, and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Tamoxifen treatment of Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice selectively abolishes PKD2 expression in myocytes.
source: These results indicate that PKD2 is expressed in myocytes of mesenteric and hindlimb arteries and aorta and that tamoxifen treatment of Pkd2fl/fl:Myh11-cre/ERT2 mice selectively abolishes PKD2 expression in myocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined RT-PCR, Western blot, and immunofluorescence data showing cell-type specific knockout.

claim: Diastolic and systolic blood pressures were both lower in Pkd2 smKO mice than in Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Telemetry indicated that diastolic and systolic blood pressures were both lower in Pkd2 smKO mice than in Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) was lower in Pkd2 smKO mice during both day and night cycles.
source: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) was lower in Pkd2 smKO mice during both day and night cycles, was sustained for days and on average was ~ 22.5% lower in Pkd2 smKO mice than in Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements over multiple days.

claim: MAP was sustained for days and on average was ~ 22.5% lower in Pkd2 smKO mice than in Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) was lower in Pkd2 smKO mice during both day and night cycles, was sustained for days and on average was ~ 22.5% lower in Pkd2 smKO mice than in Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of telemetric blood pressure data.

claim: Locomotion was similar between genotypes, indicating that the lower blood pressure in Pkd2 smKO mice was not due to inactivity.
source: Locomotion was similar between genotypes, indicating that the lower blood pressure in Pkd2 smKO mice was not due to inactivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on locomotor activity measurements showing no difference between genotypes.

claim: Cardiac output, fractional shortening, ejection fraction and heart rate were similar in Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Echocardiography indicated that cardiac output, fractional shortening, ejection fraction and heart rate were similar in Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by echocardiography measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Pkd2 smKO kidney glomeruli and tubules were normal and indistinguishable from those of Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Pkd2 smKO kidney glomeruli and tubules were normal and indistinguishable from those of Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by histological examination of kidney sections shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Plasma angiotensin II, aldosterone and ANP and plasma and urine electrolytes were similar in Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Plasma angiotensin II, aldosterone and ANP and plasma and urine electrolytes were similar in Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice (Table 1, p>0.05 for all).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA and electrolyte measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: Arterial myocyte PKD2 channels control systemic blood pressure.
source: These results demonstrate that arterial myocyte PKD2 channels control systemic blood pressure and that cardiac function and kidney anatomy and function are similar in Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the blood pressure measurements and the absence of cardiac or renal dysfunction.

claim: Cardiac function and kidney anatomy and function are similar in Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: These results demonstrate that arterial myocyte PKD2 channels control systemic blood pressure and that cardiac function and kidney anatomy and function are similar in Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on echocardiography, histology, and biochemical measurements.

claim: Intravascular pressures greater than 40 mmHg produced increasing levels of constriction in Pkd2fl/fl arteries, reaching ~ 20.9% tone at 100 mmHg.
source: Intravascular pressures greater than 40 mmHg produced increasing levels of constriction in Pkd2fl/fl arteries, reaching ~ 20.9% tone at 100 mmHg (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by myogenic tone measurements in pressurized arteries shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Pressure-induced vasoconstriction was robustly attenuated in Pkd2 smKO gastrocnemius arteries, which developed only ~ 5.4% tone at 100 mmHg or approximately one quarter of that in Pkd2fl/fl arteries.
source: In contrast, pressure-induced vasoconstriction was robustly attenuated in Pkd2 smKO gastrocnemius arteries, which developed only ~ 5.4% tone at 100 mmHg or approximately one quarter of that in Pkd2fl/fl arteries (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by myogenic tone measurements showing significant reduction in knockout arteries.

claim: The passive diameters of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO gastrocnemius arteries were similar.
source: The passive diameters of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO gastrocnemius arteries were similar (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by passive diameter measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Depolarization (60 mM K+) stimulated slightly larger vasoconstriction in Pkd2 smKO than Pkd2fl/fl gastrocnemius arteries.
source: Depolarization (60 mM K+) stimulated slightly larger vasoconstriction in Pkd2 smKO than Pkd2fl/fl gastrocnemius arteries (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by K+-induced vasoconstriction measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The small increase in CaV1.2 protein measured in gastrocnemius arteries of Pkd2 smKO mice indicates that attenuation of the myogenic response is not due to loss of voltage-dependent Ca2+ channel function.
source: These data are consistent with the small increase in CaV1.2 protein measured in gastrocnemius arteries of Pkd2 smKO mice and indicate that attenuation of the myogenic response is not due to loss of voltage-dependent Ca2+ channel function and that the reduction in systemic blood pressure may stimulate CaV1.2 expression in hindlimb arteries, but not in mesenteric arteries or aorta (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of CaV1.2 protein levels and functional vasoconstriction data.

claim: The reduction in systemic blood pressure may stimulate CaV1.2 expression in hindlimb arteries, but not in mesenteric arteries or aorta.
source: These data are consistent with the small increase in CaV1.2 protein measured in gastrocnemius arteries of Pkd2 smKO mice and indicate that attenuation of the myogenic response is not due to loss of voltage-dependent Ca2+ channel function and that the reduction in systemic blood pressure may stimulate CaV1.2 expression in hindlimb arteries, but not in mesenteric arteries or aorta (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential CaV1.2 expression patterns.

claim: Phenylephrine stimulated similar vasoconstrictions in pressurized gastrocnemius arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mice.
source: Phenylephrine stimulated similar vasoconstrictions in pressurized gastrocnemius arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by phenylephrine-induced vasoconstriction measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Angiotensin II stimulated similar vasoconstrictions in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mouse gastrocnemius arteries.
source: Angiotensin II also stimulated similar vasoconstrictions in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mouse gastrocnemius arteries (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by angiotensin II-induced vasoconstriction measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Stepwise increases in intravascular flow produced lower pressures in hindlimbs of Pkd2 smKO mice than in those of Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Stepwise increases in intravascular flow produced lower pressures in hindlimbs of Pkd2 smKO mice than in those of Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by perfused hindlimb pressure measurements shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: At a flow rate of at 2.5 ml/min the mean pressure in hindlimbs of Pkd2 smKO mice were ~ 63.2% of those in Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: For example, at a flow rate of at 2.5 ml/min the mean pressure in hindlimbs of Pkd2 smKO mice were ~ 63.2% of those in Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of perfused hindlimb pressure data.

claim: At constant flow, phenylephrine similarly increased pressure in hindlimbs of Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: In contrast, at constant flow, phenylephrine similarly increased pressure in hindlimbs of Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by phenylephrine-induced pressure measurements in perfused hindlimbs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Arterial myocyte PKD2 channels are essential for pressure-induced vasoconstriction in hindlimb arteries.
source: These data suggest that arterial myocyte PKD2 channels are essential for pressure-induced vasoconstriction, but not phenylephrine- or angiotensin II-induced vasoconstriction, in hindlimb arteries.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of PKD2 knockout on pressure-induced versus agonist-induced vasoconstriction.

claim: Arterial myocyte PKD2 channels are not essential for phenylephrine-induced vasoconstriction in hindlimb arteries.
source: These data suggest that arterial myocyte PKD2 channels are essential for pressure-induced vasoconstriction, but not phenylephrine- or angiotensin II-induced vasoconstriction, in hindlimb arteries.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the similar phenylephrine responses in both genotypes.

claim: Arterial myocyte PKD2 channels are not essential for angiotensin II-induced vasoconstriction in hindlimb arteries.
source: These data suggest that arterial myocyte PKD2 channels are essential for pressure-induced vasoconstriction, but not phenylephrine- or angiotensin II-induced vasoconstriction, in hindlimb arteries.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the similar angiotensin II responses in both genotypes.

claim: At 10 mmHg, the mean membrane potential of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO arteries were similar at ~ −59.6 and −58.5 mV, respectively.
source: At 10 mmHg, the mean membrane potential of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO arteries were similar at ~ −59.6 and −58.5 mV, respectively (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by membrane potential measurements shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Increasing intravascular pressure to 100 mmHg depolarized Pkd2fl/fl arteries by ~ 22.5 mV, but did not alter the membrane potential of arteries from Pkd2 smKO mice.
source: Increasing intravascular pressure to 100 mmHg depolarized Pkd2fl/fl arteries by ~ 22.5 mV, but did not alter the membrane potential of arteries from Pkd2 smKO mice (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by membrane potential measurements showing differential pressure-induced depolarization.

claim: Phenylephrine depolarized arteries to similar membrane potentials in both genotypes.
source: In contrast, phenylephrine depolarized arteries to similar membrane potentials in both genotypes (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by membrane potential measurements showing similar phenylephrine-induced depolarization in both genotypes.

claim: Pressure activates PKD2 channels in myocytes of hindlimb arteries, leading to depolarization and vasoconstriction.
source: These data suggest that pressure activates PKD2 channels in myocytes of hindlimb arteries, leading to depolarization and vasoconstriction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the membrane potential and vasoconstriction data.

claim: Recombinant PKD2 generates voltage-dependent, outwardly rectifying currents and is primarily a Na+-permeant channel under physiological membrane potentials and ionic gradients.
source: Recent evidence indicates that recombinant PKD2 generates voltage-dependent, outwardly rectifying currents and is primarily a Na+-permeant channel under physiological membrane potentials and ionic gradients (Shen et al., 2016; Gonzalez-Perrett et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies on recombinant PKD2.

claim: In Pkd2fl/fl myocytes, reducing bath solution osmolarity from 300 to 250 mOsm caused cell swelling and activated an outwardly rectifying ICat that increased 2.3 ± 0.3 and 3.0 ± 0.7 fold at −100 and + 100 mV, respectively.
source: In Pkd2fl/fl myocytes, reducing bath solution osmolarity from 300 to 250 mOsm caused cell swelling and activated an outwardly rectifying ICat that increased 2.3 ± 0.3 and 3.0 ± 0.7 fold at −100 and + 100 mV, respectively (p<0.05, n = 5, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Swelling-activated ICat was inhibited by Gd3+, a non-selective cation channel blocker.
source: Swelling-activated ICat was inhibited by Gd3+, a non-selective cation channel blocker (Figure 4C,D,E).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recordings showing Gd3+ inhibition of swelling-activated currents.

claim: The mean reversal potential for ICat was similar in isotonic (−0.2 ± 1.3 mV) and hypotonic solutions (0.1 ± 3.8 mV; p>0.05), suggesting that swelling activated a INa.
source: The mean reversal potential for ICat was similar in isotonic (−0.2 ± 1.3 mV) and hypotonic solutions (0.1 ± 3.8 mV; p>0.05), suggesting that swelling activated a INa.
evidence: This is an inference based on reversal potential measurements suggesting Na+ permeability.

claim: In a hypotonic bath solution, a reduction in bath [Na+] from 115 to 40 mM shifted the Erev to −14.6 ± 0.5 mV in Pkd2fl/fl myocytes.
source: In a hypotonic bath solution, a reduction in bath [Na+] from 115 to 40 mM shifted the Erev to −14.6 ± 0.5 mV in Pkd2fl/fl myocytes (n = 5, p<0.05 versus Erev in 250 mOsm) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recordings with Na+ substitution shown in Figure 4F.

claim: When adjusted for the liquid junction potential caused by the solution change (+6.9 mV), the corrected Erev is −21.5 ± 0.5 mV, which is similar to the calculated ENa (−24.2 mV).
source: When adjusted for the liquid junction potential caused by the solution change (+6.9 mV), the corrected Erev is −21.5 ± 0.5 mV, which is similar to the calculated ENa (−24.2 mV).
evidence: This is an inference based on reversal potential measurements and calculations confirming Na+ selectivity.

claim: Reducing bath Na+ decreased inward current and increased outward current.
source: Reducing bath Na+ also decreased inward current and increased outward current.
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recordings showing changes in current with Na+ substitution.

claim: Swelling did not activate a ICat in hindlimb artery myocytes of Pkd2 smKO mice.
source: In contrast, swelling did not activate a ICat (p<0.05, n = 5), nor did Gd3+ alter ICat when applied in hypotonic bath solution, in hindlimb artery myocytes of Pkd2 smKO mice (Figure 4C,D,E).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recordings showing absence of swelling-activated currents in knockout myocytes.

claim: Phenylephrine activated similar amplitude ICats in hindlimb artery myocytes of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mice.
source: In further contrast to the differential effects of cell swelling, phenylephrine activated similar amplitude ICats in hindlimb artery myocytes of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recordings showing similar phenylephrine-activated currents in both genotypes.

claim: Cell swelling activates PKD2 channels, leading to a Na+ current in hindlimb artery myocytes.
source: These data indicate that cell swelling activates PKD2 channels, leading to a Na+ current in hindlimb artery myocytes, whereas phenylephrine does not activate PKD2 channels in this cell type.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of swelling and phenylephrine on currents in control versus knockout myocytes.

claim: Phenylephrine does not activate PKD2 channels in hindlimb artery myocytes.
source: These data indicate that cell swelling activates PKD2 channels, leading to a Na+ current in hindlimb artery myocytes, whereas phenylephrine does not activate PKD2 channels in this cell type.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the similar phenylephrine-activated currents in both genotypes.

claim: Pressure- and depolarization-induced vasoconstriction was similar in mesenteric arteries of Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: In contrast to the robust attenuation of myogenic vasoconstriction in gastrocnemius arteries of Pkd2 smKO mice, pressure- and depolarization-induced vasoconstriction was similar in mesenteric arteries of Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by myogenic tone and K+-induced vasoconstriction measurements in mesenteric arteries.

claim: Myogenic tone was similar regardless of whether third, fourth, or fifth-order Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mouse mesenteric arteries were studied.
source: Myogenic tone was similar regardless of whether third, fourth, or fifth-order Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mouse mesenteric arteries were studied (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by myogenic tone measurements in different orders of mesenteric arteries shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Passive diameter of mesenteric arteries was not altered by myocyte PKD2 knockout.
source: Passive diameter of mesenteric arteries was not altered by myocyte PKD2 knockout (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by passive diameter measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The differential contribution of myocyte PKD2 channels to pressure-induced vasoconstriction in gastrocnemius and mesenteric arteries was not due to size, as passive diameters of first-order gastrocnemius and third-order mesenteric arteries were similar.
source: The differential contribution of myocyte PKD2 channels to pressure-induced vasoconstriction in gastrocnemius and mesenteric arteries was not due to size, as passive diameters of first-order gastrocnemius and third-order mesenteric arteries were similar (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on passive diameter measurements showing similar vessel sizes.

claim: Phenylephrine-induced isometric contractions in mesenteric artery rings of Pkd2 smKO mice were smaller than those in Pkd2fl/fl controls.
source: Phenylephrine-induced isometric contractions in mesenteric artery (first- and second-order) rings of Pkd2 smKO mice were smaller than those in Pkd2fl/fl controls (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by wire myography measurements shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: With 1 µM phenylephrine, contractions in Pkd2 smKO arteries were ~ 15.3% of those in Pkd2fl/fl arteries, with maximal phenylephrine-induced contraction ~ 57.3% of that in Pkd2fl/fl arteries.
source: For instance, with 1 µM phenylephrine, contractions in Pkd2 smKO arteries were ~ 15.3% of those in Pkd2fl/fl arteries, with maximal phenylephrine-induced contraction ~ 57.3% of that in Pkd2fl/fl arteries (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of phenylephrine-induced contractions.

claim: The mean concentration of phenylephrine-induced half-maximal contraction (EC50, µM) was slightly higher in Pkd2 smKO (2.4 ± 0.2) than Pkd2fl/fl (1.1 ± 0.3) arteries.
source: The mean concentration of phenylephrine-induced half-maximal contraction (EC50, µM) was slightly higher in Pkd2 smKO (2.4 ± 0.2) than Pkd2fl/fl (1.1 ± 0.3) arteries (p<0.05, Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by EC50 calculations from concentration-response curves.

claim: In pressurized (80 mmHg) mesenteric (fourth- and fifth-order) arteries of Pkd2 smKO mice, phenylephrine-induced vasoconstrictions were between ~ 50.9% and 64.8% of those in Pkd2fl/fl controls.
source: In pressurized (80 mmHg) mesenteric (fourth- and fifth-order) arteries of Pkd2 smKO mice, phenylephrine-induced vasoconstrictions were between ~ 50.9% and 64.8% of those in Pkd2fl/fl controls (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by phenylephrine-induced vasoconstriction measurements in pressurized mesenteric arteries.

claim: Similar results were obtained with endothelium-denuded mesenteric arteries, indicating that attenuated vasoconstriction to phenylephrine was due to loss of PKD2 in myocytes.
source: Similar results were obtained with endothelium-denuded mesenteric arteries, indicating that attenuated vasoconstriction to phenylephrine was due to loss of PKD2 in myocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is an inference based on experiments with endothelium-denuded arteries showing similar phenylephrine attenuation.

claim: Angiotensin II-induced constriction was not different between Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mesenteric arteries.
source: In contrast to attenuated phenylephrine-mediated vasoconstriction, angiotensin II-induced constriction was not different between Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mesenteric arteries (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by angiotensin II-induced vasoconstriction measurements showing no difference between genotypes.

claim: Arterial myocyte PKD2 channels are activated by distinct vasoconstrictor stimuli in arteries of different tissues.
source: These data indicate that arterial myocyte PKD2 channels are activated by distinct vasoconstrictor stimuli in arteries of different tissues, contributing to α1-adrenoceptor-mediated vasoconstriction in mesenteric arteries and essential for the myogenic response in hindlimb arteries.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of pressure and phenylephrine in hindlimb versus mesenteric arteries.

claim: Arterial myocyte PKD2 channels contribute to α1-adrenoceptor-mediated vasoconstriction in mesenteric arteries.
source: These data indicate that arterial myocyte PKD2 channels are activated by distinct vasoconstrictor stimuli in arteries of different tissues, contributing to α1-adrenoceptor-mediated vasoconstriction in mesenteric arteries and essential for the myogenic response in hindlimb arteries.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the attenuated phenylephrine responses in knockout mesenteric arteries.

claim: Arterial myocyte PKD2 channels are essential for the myogenic response in hindlimb arteries.
source: These data indicate that arterial myocyte PKD2 channels are activated by distinct vasoconstrictor stimuli in arteries of different tissues, contributing to α1-adrenoceptor-mediated vasoconstriction in mesenteric arteries and essential for the myogenic response in hindlimb arteries.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the abolished myogenic response in knockout hindlimb arteries.

claim: At an intravascular pressure of 10 mmHg, the membrane potential of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mesenteric arteries was similar.
source: At an intravascular pressure of 10 mmHg, the membrane potential of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mesenteric arteries was similar (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by membrane potential measurements shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: An increase in pressure to 80 mmHg stimulated a similar depolarization in mesenteric arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mice, to ~39.7 and 36.7 mV, respectively.
source: An increase in pressure to 80 mmHg stimulated a similar depolarization in mesenteric arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mice, to ~39.7 and 36.7 mV, respectively (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by membrane potential measurements showing similar pressure-induced depolarization in both genotypes.

claim: Phenylephrine application further depolarized Pkd2fl/fl mesenteric arteries by ~19.9 mV, but did not change the membrane potential of Pkd2 smKO arteries.
source: Phenylephrine application further depolarized Pkd2fl/fl mesenteric arteries by ~19.9 mV, but did not change the membrane potential of Pkd2 smKO arteries (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by membrane potential measurements showing differential phenylephrine-induced depolarization.

claim: In Pkd2fl/fl cells, phenylephrine activated outwardly rectifying ICat, increasing density ~ 1.43 and 1.57-fold at −100 mV and + 100 mV, respectively.
source: In Pkd2fl/fl cells, phenylephrine activated outwardly rectifying ICat, increasing density ~ 1.43 and 1.57-fold at −100 mV and + 100 mV, respectively (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: In the presence of phenylephrine, a reduction in bath [Na]o from 140 to 40 mM shifted the Erev from 0.5 ± 0.5 to −23.2 ± 1.6 mV in Pkd2fl/fl myocytes.
source: In the presence of phenylephrine, a reduction in bath [Na]o from 140 to 40 mM shifted the Erev from 0.5 ± 0.5 to −23.2 ± 1.6 mV in Pkd2fl/fl myocytes (n = 5, p<0.05 versus PE/low Na+).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recordings with Na+ substitution.

claim: When corrected for the liquid junction potential (+5.6 mV) caused by the change in bath [Na]o, this Erev is −28.8 ± 1.6 mV, which is similar to calculated ENa (−32.8 mV) under these conditions.
source: When corrected for the liquid junction potential (+5.6 mV) caused by the change in bath [Na]o, this Erev is −28.8 ± 1.6 mV, which is similar to calculated ENa (−32.8 mV) under these conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on reversal potential measurements and calculations confirming Na+ selectivity.

claim: Reducing bath Na+ reduced inward current and increased outward current.
source: Reducing bath Na+ also reduced inward current and increased outward current.
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recordings showing changes in current with Na+ substitution.

claim: The subsequent addition of Gd3+ reduced current density to ~ 44.9% and 20.7% of that in phenylephrine/40 mM Na+at −100 and + 100 mV, respectively.
source: The subsequent addition of Gd3+ reduced current density to ~ 44.9% and 20.7% of that in phenylephrine/40 mM Na+at −100 and + 100 mV, respectively (n = 5, p<0.05, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recordings showing Gd3+ inhibition of phenylephrine-activated currents.

claim: Phenylephrine did not alter ICat in Pkd2 smKO myocytes.
source: In contrast to effects in Pkd2fl/fl myocytes, phenylephrine did not alter ICat in Pkd2 smKO myocytes (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recordings showing no phenylephrine effect in knockout myocytes.

claim: Swelling activated similar amplitude ICat in mesenteric artery myocytes of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mice.
source: In further contrast to the differential effects of phenylephrine, swelling activated similar amplitude ICat in mesenteric artery myocytes of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 smKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp recordings showing similar swelling-activated currents in both genotypes.

claim: Phenylephrine activates PKD2 channels, leading to a INa in mesenteric artery myocytes.
source: These data indicate that phenylephrine activates PKD2 channels, leading to a INa in mesenteric artery myocytes, whereas cell swelling does not activate PKD2 channels in mesenteric artery myocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of phenylephrine in control versus knockout myocytes.

claim: Cell swelling does not activate PKD2 channels in mesenteric artery myocytes.
source: These data indicate that phenylephrine activates PKD2 channels, leading to a INa in mesenteric artery myocytes, whereas cell swelling does not activate PKD2 channels in mesenteric artery myocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the similar swelling-activated currents in both genotypes.

claim: Angiotensin II steadily increased MAP to a plateau of ~155.6 mmHg in Pkd2fl/fl mice and to ~ 134.6 mmHg in Pkd2 smKO mice.
source: Angiotensin II steadily increased MAP to a plateau of ~155.6 mmHg in Pkd2fl/fl mice and to ~ 134.6 mmHg in Pkd2 smKO mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements during angiotensin II infusion shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The angiotensin II-induced increase in MAP (ΔMAP) was ~ 25.6% smaller in Pkd2 smKO than Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: The angiotensin II-induced increase in MAP (ΔMAP) was ~ 25.6% smaller in Pkd2 smKO than Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of the blood pressure increase during angiotensin II infusion.

claim: Saline infusion did not alter blood pressure in either Pkd2 smKO or Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Saline infusion did not alter blood pressure in either Pkd2 smKO or Pkd2fl/fl mice.
evidence: This is supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements during saline infusion.

claim: Myocyte PKD2 channel knockout reduces both the absolute systemic blood pressure and the increase in blood pressure during hypertension.
source: These data indicate that myocyte PKD2 channel knockout reduces both the absolute systemic blood pressure and the increase in blood pressure during hypertension.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the blood pressure measurements in normotensive and hypertensive conditions.

claim: PKD2 total protein in mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of angiotensin II-induced hypertensive mice were ~ 149.2% and 143.4%, respectively, of those in normotensive mice.
source: PKD2 total protein in mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of angiotensin II-induced hypertensive mice were ~ 149.2% and 143.4%, respectively, of those in normotensive mice (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot quantification of total PKD2 protein shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Surface PKD2 protein in mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of hypertensive mice were ~ 150.3% and 145.9% of those in controls.
source: Arterial biotinylation revealed that surface PKD2 protein in mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of hypertensive mice were also ~ 150.3% and 145.9% of those in controls (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is supported by biotinylation assays quantifying surface PKD2 protein shown in Figures 7D and 7E.

claim: Cellular distribution of PKD2 was similar in mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of normotensive and hypertensive mice, with ~ 85% of protein located in the plasma membrane.
source: In contrast, cellular distribution of PKD2 was similar in mesenteric and hindlimb arteries of normotensive and hypertensive mice, with ~ 85% of protein located in the plasma membrane (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of surface versus intracellular PKD2 distribution shown in Figure 7F.

claim: During hypertension, an increase in total PKD2 protein leads to an increase in the abundance of surface PKD2 channels.
source: These data indicate that during hypertension, an increase in total PKD2 protein leads to an increase in the abundance of surface PKD2 channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proportional increases in total and surface PKD2 protein during hypertension.

claim: Phenylephrine-induced vasoconstrictions in angiotensin II-treated Pkd2 smKO mouse arteries were between ~67.6% and 71.1% of those in Pkd2fl/fl arteries.
source: Phenylephrine-induced vasoconstrictions in angiotensin II-treated Pkd2 smKO mouse arteries were between ~67.6% and 71.1% of those in Pkd2fl/fl arteries (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by phenylephrine-induced vasoconstriction measurements in hypertensive mice shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Myogenic tone was similar in arteries of angiotensin II-treated Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: In contrast, myogenic tone was similar in arteries of angiotensin II-treated Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by myogenic tone measurements in hypertensive mice shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Knockout of arterial myocyte PKD2 channels attenuates phenylephrine-induced vasoconstriction during hypertension.
source: These results indicate that knockout of arterial myocyte PKD2 channels attenuates phenylephrine-induced vasoconstriction during hypertension.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the attenuated phenylephrine responses in knockout hypertensive mice.

claim: Hypertension does not promote the emergence of a mechanism by which PKD2 channels contribute to the myogenic response in mesenteric arteries.
source: These data also suggest that hypertension does not promote the emergence of a mechanism by which PKD2 channels contribute to the myogenic response in mesenteric arteries.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar myogenic tone in both genotypes during hypertension.

claim: In saline-treated Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice, the wall-to-lumen ratio of mesenteric arteries was similar.
source: In saline-treated Pkd2 smKO and Pkd2fl/fl mice, the wall-to-lumen ratio of mesenteric arteries was similar (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis of arterial wall-to-lumen ratios shown in Figures 8C and 8D.

claim: Angiotensin II infusion increased the artery wall-to-lumen ratio ~2.9 fold in Pkd2fl/fl mice, but only 1.3-fold in Pkd2 smKO mice, or ~89.6% less.
source: Angiotensin II infusion increased the artery wall-to-lumen ratio ~2.9 fold in Pkd2fl/fl mice, but only 1.3-fold in Pkd2 smKO mice, or ~89.6% less (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of arterial remodeling shown in Figures 8C and 8D.

claim: PKD2 knockout in myocytes attenuates arterial remodeling during hypertension.
source: These data suggest that PKD2 knockout in myocytes attenuates arterial remodeling during hypertension.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reduced wall-to-lumen ratio in knockout hypertensive mice.

claim: Systemic blood pressure is determined, in part, by arterial smooth muscle cells (myocytes).
source: Systemic blood pressure is determined, in part, by arterial smooth muscle cells (myocytes).
evidence: This is established knowledge in cardiovascular physiology.

claim: Several Transient Receptor Potential (TRP) channels are proposed to be expressed in arterial myocytes.
source: Several Transient Receptor Potential (TRP) channels are proposed to be expressed in arterial myocytes, but it is unclear if these proteins control physiological blood pressure and contribute to hypertension in vivo.
evidence: This is based on previous literature suggesting TRP channel expression in arterial myocytes.

claim: It is unclear if TRP channels control physiological blood pressure and contribute to hypertension in vivo.
source: Several Transient Receptor Potential (TRP) channels are proposed to be expressed in arterial myocytes, but it is unclear if these proteins control physiological blood pressure and contribute to hypertension in vivo.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: Intravascular pressure and α1-adrenoceptors activate PKD2 channels in arterial myocytes of different systemic organs.
source: Using this model, we show that intravascular pressure and α1-adrenoceptors activate PKD2 channels in arterial myocytes of different systemic organs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: PKD2 channel activation in arterial myocytes leads to an inward Na+ current, membrane depolarization and vasoconstriction.
source: PKD2 channel activation in arterial myocytes leads to an inward Na+ current, membrane depolarization and vasoconstriction.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by electrophysiology and myography experiments.

claim: Inducible, smooth muscle cell-specific PKD2 knockout lowers both physiological blood pressure and hypertension.
source: Inducible, smooth muscle cell-specific PKD2 knockout lowers both physiological blood pressure and hypertension and prevents pathological arterial remodeling during hypertension.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements.

claim: Inducible, smooth muscle cell-specific PKD2 knockout prevents pathological arterial remodeling during hypertension.
source: Inducible, smooth muscle cell-specific PKD2 knockout lowers both physiological blood pressure and hypertension and prevents pathological arterial remodeling during hypertension.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by histological analysis.

claim: Arterial myocyte PKD2 controls systemic blood pressure.
source: Thus, arterial myocyte PKD2 controls systemic blood pressure and targeting this TRP channel reduces high blood pressure.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the blood pressure measurements in knockout mice.

claim: Targeting PKD2 channel reduces high blood pressure.
source: Thus, arterial myocyte PKD2 controls systemic blood pressure and targeting this TRP channel reduces high blood pressure.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the blood pressure measurements in hypertensive knockout mice.

claim: Membrane potential is a primary determinant of arterial contractility.
source: Membrane potential is a primary determinant of arterial contractility (Nelson et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge in vascular physiology supported by a citation.

claim: Depolarization activates myocyte voltage-dependent calcium (Ca2+) channels (CaV), leading to an increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration [Ca2+]i and vasoconstriction.
source: Depolarization activates myocyte voltage-dependent calcium (Ca2+) channels (CaV), leading to an increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration [Ca2+]i and vasoconstriction.
evidence: This is established knowledge in vascular physiology.

claim: Hyperpolarization reduces [Ca2+]i, resulting in vasodilation.
source: In contrast, hyperpolarization reduces [Ca2+]i, resulting in vasodilation (Nelson et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge in vascular physiology supported by a citation.

claim: Transient Receptor Potential (TRP) channels constitute a family of ~28 proteins that are subdivided into six different classes.
source: Transient Receptor Potential (TRP) channels constitute a family of ~28 proteins that are subdivided into six different classes, including polycystin (TRPP), canonical (TRPC), vanilloid (TRPV), ankyrin (TRPA), and melastatin (TRPM) (Earley and Brayden, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TRP channel classification supported by a citation.

claim: Approximately thirteen different TRP channels may be expressed in arterial myocytes, including PKD2, TRPC1, TRPC3-6, TRPV1-4, TRPA1, TRPM4 and TRPM8.
source: Experiments performed using cultured and non-cultured cells and whole arteries, which contain multiple different cell types, have suggested that approximately thirteen different TRP channels may be expressed in arterial myocytes, including PKD2 (also termed TRPP1), TRPC1, TRPC3-6, TRPV1-4, TRPA1, TRPM4 and TRPM8 (Earley and Brayden, 2015).
evidence: This is based on previous literature suggesting TRP channel expression in arterial myocytes, supported by a citation.

claim: Blood pressure measurements in constitutive, global TRPC6, TRPM4 and TRPV4 channel knockout mice produced inconsistent results or generated complex findings that were associated with compensatory mechanisms.
source: Blood pressure measurements in constitutive, global TRPC6, TRPM4 and TRPV4 channel knockout mice produced inconsistent results or generated complex findings that were associated with compensatory mechanisms (Mathar et al., 2010; Dietrich et al., 2005; Nishijima et al., 2014; Earley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on previous studies of TRP channel knockout mice, supported by citations.

claim: The contribution of arterial myocyte TRP channels to physiological systemic blood pressure and pathological changes in blood pressure are unclear.
source: Thus, the contribution of arterial myocyte TRP channels to physiological systemic blood pressure and pathological changes in blood pressure are unclear.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap based on the inconsistent findings from previous studies.

claim: PKD2 is a six transmembrane domain protein with cytoplasmic N and C termini.
source: PKD2 is a six transmembrane domain protein with cytoplasmic N and C termini (Shen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PKD2 structure supported by a citation.

claim: PKD2 is expressed in myocytes of rat and human cerebral arteries, mouse and human mesenteric arteries and in porcine whole aorta.
source: PKD2 is expressed in myocytes of rat and human cerebral arteries, mouse and human mesenteric arteries and in porcine whole aorta (Griffin et al., 1997; Torres et al., 2001; Narayanan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on previous studies showing PKD2 expression in various arteries, supported by citations.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of PKD2 inhibited pressure-induced vasoconstriction (myogenic tone) in cerebral arteries.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of PKD2 inhibited pressure-induced vasoconstriction (myogenic tone) in cerebral arteries (Narayanan et al., 2013; Sharif-Naeini et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on previous studies using RNAi knockdown, supported by citations.

claim: In global, constitutive PKD2+/- mice, an increase in actin and myosin expression lead to larger phenylephrine-induced contractions in aorta and mesenteric arteries.
source: In global, constitutive PKD2+/- mice, an increase in actin and myosin expression lead to larger phenylephrine-induced contractions in aorta and mesenteric arteries (Qian et al., 2007; Du et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on previous studies in PKD2+/- mice, supported by citations.

claim: It has been proposed that arterial myocyte PKD2 channels inhibit myogenic tone in mesenteric arteries.
source: It has also been proposed that arterial myocyte PKD2 channels inhibit myogenic tone in mesenteric arteries (Sharif-Naeini et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on a previous study proposing an inhibitory role for PKD2, supported by a citation.

claim: In vitro studies have generated variable findings regarding physiological functions of arterial myocyte PKD2 channels.
source: Thus, in vitro studies have generated variable findings regarding physiological functions of arterial myocyte PKD2 channels.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the inconsistent findings from previous studies cited.

claim: Inducible and cell-specific PKD2 channel knockout in myocytes reduces systemic blood pressure.
source: We show that inducible and cell-specific PKD2 channel knockout in myocytes reduces systemic blood pressure.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements.

claim: PKD2 channels are upregulated during hypertension.
source: We also show that PKD2 channels are upregulated during hypertension and that myocyte PKD2 knockout causes vasodilation, attenuates remodeling of the arterial wall and reduces high blood pressure during hypertension.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by Western blot and biotinylation data.

claim: Myocyte PKD2 knockout causes vasodilation during hypertension.
source: We also show that PKD2 channels are upregulated during hypertension and that myocyte PKD2 knockout causes vasodilation, attenuates remodeling of the arterial wall and reduces high blood pressure during hypertension.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by myography experiments in hypertensive mice.

claim: Myocyte PKD2 knockout attenuates remodeling of the arterial wall during hypertension.
source: We also show that PKD2 channels are upregulated during hypertension and that myocyte PKD2 knockout causes vasodilation, attenuates remodeling of the arterial wall and reduces high blood pressure during hypertension.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by histological analysis of arterial wall-to-lumen ratios.

claim: Myocyte PKD2 knockout reduces high blood pressure during hypertension.
source: We also show that PKD2 channels are upregulated during hypertension and that myocyte PKD2 knockout causes vasodilation, attenuates remodeling of the arterial wall and reduces high blood pressure during hypertension.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements in hypertensive mice.

claim: Arterial myocyte PKD2 channels control physiological blood pressure and are upregulated during hypertension, contributing to the blood pressure elevation.
source: In summary, our study indicates that PKD2 channels in systemic artery myocytes control physiological blood pressure and are upregulated during hypertension, contributing to the blood pressure elevation.
evidence: This is the primary conclusion of the study based on all the experimental findings.
